#81802. Breaking: Earth’s ancient oceans may have fooled scientists about its oxygen history

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1068 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Earth’s ancient oceans may have fooled scientists about its oxygen history

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1068 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For billions of years, Earth's atmosphere contained almost no oxygen, making the planet vastly different from the world we know today.
  • Two geochemists from Chengdu University of Technology have presented this revised timeline in The Innovation.
  • Scientists have traditionally reconstructed Earth's atmospheric oxygen levels using chemical clues preserved in ancient ocean sediments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For billions of years, Earth's atmosphere contained almost no oxygen, making the planet vastly different from the world we know today. A new scientific analysis suggests that oxygen accumulated in the atmosphere during three major stages, while the deep oceans took much longer to catch up. In some cases, the delay stretched across hundreds of millions of years, with the final transition involving a gap of roughly 600 million years.

Two geochemists from Chengdu University of Technology have presented this revised timeline in The Innovation. Their findings challenge the traditional understanding of Earth's oxygen history by examining chemical evidence that reflects conditions in the ancient atmosphere rather than relying primarily on measurements of ocean chemistry.

Ancient Rocks Reveal a Different Oxygen Timeline.

Scientists have traditionally reconstructed Earth's atmospheric oxygen levels using chemical clues preserved in ancient ocean sediments. However, the amount of oxygen in seawater is influenced by many factors besides the atmosphere, including nutrient availability, biological productivity, ocean circulation, and the shapes of ocean basins. This makes ocean chemistry an imperfect guide to conditions in the air.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers instead focused on sulfate, a chemical compound that can preserve a distinctive signal from atmospheric oxygen. Reactions involving oxygen, ozone, and carbon dioxide in the atmosphere produce an unusual shortage of the oxygen isotope oxygen-17. When sulfide minerals undergo weathering, this chemical fingerprint is transferred into sulfate, which can eventually become preserved in sedimentary rocks. By examining these signatures, scientists can gain a more direct picture of how atmospheric oxygen changed over time.

According to this evidence, Earth's first major increase in oxygen occurred during the Great Oxidation Event, between 2.4 billion and 2.1 billion years ago. Atmospheric oxygen rose from less than one-millionth of today's concentration to somewhere between 0.1% and 10% of modern levels.

The second major increase took place approximately 1.3 billion to 1.0 billion years ago, followed by a third between 440 million and 410 million years ago. Both occurred earlier than conventional timelines suggest.

Under this interpretation, the well-known Neoproterozoic and Paleozoic oxygenation events, traditionally dated to 800 million to 500 million years ago and 420 million to 360 million years ago, mainly reflect delayed changes in ocean oxygen levels. The oceans responded roughly 200 million and 30 million years after the corresponding atmospheric increases.

Earth's Atmosphere and Oceans Did Not Always Change Together.

Despite these major increases, oxygen remained relatively scarce throughout much of Earth's history. Models based on the isotope evidence suggest that atmospheric oxygen during the middle Proterozoic reached only about 0.1% to 1% of present-day levels.

Another clue comes from the fossil record of charcoal. Because charcoal formation requires atmospheric oxygen concentrations of approximately three-quarters of modern levels, its absence from older rocks suggests that oxygen remained too scarce to support widespread burning. Charcoal first appears in the geological record around 420 million years ago.

It has been revealed that the researchers also highlight a surprising relationship between oxygen in the atmosphere and oxygen in the oceans. Over extremely long periods, the two generally increased together. However, on timescales of around a million years, they could move in opposite directions.

When additional oxygen entered the oceans, it could react with accumulated organic carbon and sulfide, consuming oxygen in the process. These reactions could reduce the amount of oxygen remaining in the atmosphere.

In a recent development, as a result, some chemical signals previously interpreted as evidence of rising oxygen may actually record periods when atmospheric oxygen was declining. This possibility could change how scientists interpret major fluctuations in Earth's ancient oxygen record.

Oxygen-Rich Oases Existed Billions of Years Ago.

The spread of oxygen through Earth's oceans was also far from uniform. The researchers describe two major sources of oxygen in seawater: oxygen produced locally by photosynthetic microorganisms and oxygen absorbed from the atmosphere.

According to recent reports, the first process created isolated pockets of oxygen-rich water as early as 3 billion years ago, possibly even earlier. These small oxygenated environments existed during the Archean, when the atmosphere and most of the oceans still contained very little free oxygen.

Industry observers note that as atmospheric oxygen levels gradually increased, oxygen entering seawater from the air became more notable. Eventually, this atmospheric supply overtook local biological production as the dominant mechanism driving widespread ocean oxygenation.

It has been revealed that even then, the transformation was remarkably slow. According to the proposed timeline, the deep ocean did not become fully oxygenated until approximately 410 million years ago, long after oxygen had begun accumulating in the atmosphere.

How Rising Oxygen Changed the Evolution of Life.

These findings also offer a new perspective on the relationship between oxygen and the evolution of complex organisms.

When Earth's atmosphere contained virtually no oxygen, its absence placed a major restriction on oxygen-dependent life. During the Proterozoic, increasing oxygen availability gradually made new environments accessible, although concentrations continued to fluctuate as early animals evolved.

Rather than acting as a single trigger for complex life, oxygen initially provided opportunities for biological innovation. Only after the third major atmospheric increase did higher oxygen levels become a powerful force supporting greater biological complexity.

This later transformation helped create conditions favorable for larger animals, more active predators, and organisms capable of occupying deeper marine environments.

The researchers acknowledge that important uncertainties remain. The available isotope record does not capture every change in detail, and absolute atmospheric oxygen concentrations after 1 billion years ago remain difficult to establish. Additional increases or decreases may have occurred without leaving sufficiently clear chemical evidence to identify them.

According to recent reports, nevertheless, the analysis proposes a major revision to the sequence of events that transformed Earth into an oxygen-rich planet. Rather than the oceans becoming oxygenated first and the atmosphere following, the evidence suggests that atmospheric oxygen increased well before the deep oceans responded.

That prolonged delay may have played an key role in shaping the environments where complex life emerged and evolved.

Five women killed every hour by family members or partners — UN report

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (382 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dw

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Around 47,000 women and girls — or five every hour — were killed by intimate partners or family members in 2025, according to a United Nations report released on Tuesday.
  • This figure equates to around 60% of women and girls who were victims of intentional homicides last year, the report mentioned ahead of the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women on November 25.
  • Recent findings suggest that the total fatalities were calculated based on statistics from 122 countries and territories.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Around 47,000 women and girls — or five every hour — were killed by intimate partners or family members in 2025, according to a United Nations report released on Tuesday.

This figure equates to around 60% of women and girls who were victims of intentional homicides last year, the report mentioned ahead of the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women on November 25.

Recent findings suggest that the total fatalities were calculated based on statistics from 122 countries and territories. They translate to an average of 129 women and girls killed by their close social circle each day.

Africa recorded the highest number of femicides, at 22,100. Asia followed, with 15,100 victims, ahead of the Americas with 7,400, Europe with 2,100 and Oceania with 300.

Femicide is a hate crime broadly defined as "the intentional killing of women or girls because they are female.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The report also found that although global homicide rates have declined, femicide rates have fallen at a slower pace, particularly in the Americas and Europe.

According to the UN, this highlights the barriers women often face in accessing the justice system and that "these crimes are deeply rooted in social norms and gender stereotypes.".

Nearly one in three women worldwide have experienced physical or sexual violence, yet only 7% reported it to the police, a separate UN Women report found.

According to estimates by UN Women and the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC, the number of women and girls killed by a family member or an intimate partner has wavered between 45,000 and 51,000 over the past several years.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

"Frightening attitudes, social norms, and the failure of institutional safeguards create an environment in which killing a wife, daughter, mother, or sister becomes 'tolerable,'" UNODC director Monica Juma said. "Changing this reality calls for sustained action across all levels of society.".

Sima Bahous, executive director of UN Women, said that the world needed to "act urgently to ensure no warning sign is ignored, no survivor is left without protection, and no perpetrator escapes accountability.".

Your guide to the Disney+ and Hulu merger: When its coming, what to expect, and how much it will cost

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the marrying of the Disney+ and Hulu apps is finally coming to fruition after a years-long effort.
  • Recent findings suggest that disney execs noted the merger is "nearly complete" in their earnings call.
  • In addition to the unified Disney+ and Hulu experience, Disney also plans to introduce creator content to the platform through its recent agreement with TikTok.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the marrying of the Disney+ and Hulu apps is finally coming to fruition after a years-long effort. By the end of the 2026, we'll have a unified app, according to Disney CEO Josh D'Amaro.

Recent findings suggest that disney execs noted the merger is "nearly complete" in their earnings call. Although there's no exact date specified, the app unification will happen before the end of 2026. Sometime in December, you can expect an official announcement and enhancement. More intends to further enhance the integrated experience are also on deck for the spring.

In addition to the unified Disney+ and Hulu experience, Disney also plans to introduce creator content to the platform through its recent agreement with TikTok. The rollout will strategically coincide with the Avengers: Doomsday theatrical release on Dec. 18. More vertical video, live sports, and podcasts will also be added to the Disney+ platform, as the app continues to explore emerging content styles.

In a recent development, this is the million dollar question. Considering the app just raised prices — for standalone subscriptions as well as some bundles — in September 2026, we don't expect the cost to change too much when the integrated app releases in December. Standalone subscriptions jumped from $11.99 to $12.49 with ads and from $18.99 to $21.49 without. Meanwhile, the Disney+ and Hulu Basic bundle remained unchanged at $12.99, while the Premium bundle went up just two bucks from $19.99 to $21.99 per month.

Sources indicate that it appears that by raising the standalone costs to nearly the same price as the bundle, the strategy is to push consumers to the bundle. The bundle is essentially the same thing as the integrated app will be, so we're expecting the price to remain pretty much on par: $12.99 with ads and $21.99 without. Of course, we'll sound the alarm if there's any major changes.

Sources indicate that black Friday streaming deals are live through Nov. 30 and I highly recommend jumping on the Disney+ and Hulu bundle deal while you can. The streamer is offering 12 months of the Basic bundle with ads for just $4.99 per month or the Premium ad-free bundle for only $14.99 per month.

By nabbing this discount, you'll bypass any potential price increases that may arise over the next 12 months. And TBH, it's the best deal we'll see for a long while. #81798. Latest Update: International first class is over for U.S. airlines. Enter the mega business-class cabin

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1127 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: International first class is over for U.S. airlines. Enter the mega business-class cabin

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1127 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • airlines' long-haul, international first class ended this week when American Airlines' last flight with its eight-suite section landed.
  • airlines have been ditching international first-class cabins for a new top tier: larger and souped-up business classes, featuring suites with sliding doors, the design du jour.
  • According to recent reports, many travelers might not notice the difference.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The era of U.S. airlines' long-haul, international first class ended this week when American Airlines' last flight with its eight-suite section landed. In its place will be a massive business-class cabin with room for 70 passengers.

Recent findings suggest that U.S. airlines have been ditching international first-class cabins for a new top tier: larger and souped-up business classes, featuring suites with sliding doors, the design du jour. Delta Air Lines and United Airlines have already taken this step. American was the last of the U.S. airlines to still have first class on long-haul international routes.

According to recent reports, many travelers might not notice the difference. That's because of airlines' investments into business class: upcoming suites, bigger screens, better technology like device-charging pads, and improved bedding.

In a recent development, it's part of airlines' massive bet on mass luxury. Consumers have been willing to shell out more to fly comfortably, which is helping to boost airline revenue. That's all the more notable as costs of everything from fuel to airport landing fees have been rising, soaking up more of the industry's profits.

The retirement of first class ends a more-than-six-decade stretch of the jet age that in the early days included service like seat-side carving of chateaubriand and meals served on fine bone china.

A few decades ago, business class was much smaller, with two-by-two seats in some configurations, and recliners, not the lie-flat seats that dominate those cabins now.

"When you've got individual pods in biz class, and you've got a comfortable enough seat and bedding and decent wine, for a lot of people this is good enough," said Henry Harteveldt, founder of travel consulting firm Atmosphere Research Group and a former airline executive.

The over-the-top dining of the early days of international first class was a form of entertainment, long before laptops, personal seat-back screens and in-flight Wi-Fi, or even the promise of sleep on lie-flat beds, but customers still eat lots on board, Harteveldt remarked.

"People say they want to sleep but then they stay up and they eat every morsel," he noted. "They're hypocrites.".

There was still a hefty price gap between first and business.

A flight between Los Angeles and London on American's Boeing 777-300ER this week went for $12,994 in business class for a one-way ticket and $15,669 for a first-class seat.

American's last flight with international first class departed Friday morning local time in Sydney, bound for Los Angeles.

It has been revealed that its new cabin on its Boeing 777-300ERs will feature 70 business-class suites, the most of any U.S. airline. Pre-overhaul, the cabins had been operating with eight first-class suites and 52 pods in business, though the remodeling is ongoing. American is also flying a subfleet of 787-9 Dreamliners that have 51 business-class suites. (United is putting 64 new suites on that aircraft.).

Part of the allure is that some companies allow employees to book business-class tickets, but not first class.

American Airlines told CNBC it's growing its business-class cabins across the fleet. It's evaluating increasing the number of suites on its smaller long-haul jets, the Boeing 787-8 Dreamliners, from 20 currently to somewhere in the 30s.

Industry observers note that "You don't have enough seats to make the seat cost competitive," Nat Pieper, American's chief commercial officer, said in an interview this month. "So what you need to do to make that airplane work is it's got to be a yield play. You need more business-class seats.".

Differences between first and business classes on American lately came down to details.

On American's first-class long-haul section, passengers got olives with warm nuts to accompany their beverage early in the flight, while there were no olives for business class.

First class got a soup; business did not. First class got a warm dessert served a la mode in addition to the cold dessert or fruit and cheese plate both cabins were offered.

And there was no memory foam lumbar pillow for business class like there was in first, American said. But otherwise, the experiences were fairly similar for passengers. They still got better food options and service than economy passengers, along with their bigger seats, early boarding and lounge access.

Recent findings suggest that "It's not like the bed can go any flatter than 180 degrees," Harteveldt remarked. "The bedding can be thicker, and the food nicer.".

Delta and United have already replaced international, long-haul first class with dozens of their Delta One and Polaris business lie-flat suites, respectively, each of which is getting upgrades now.

According to recent reports, american will continue offering a separate lie-flat first class on its Airbus A321T subfleet it uses for domestic cross-country flying until early 2027. But then that goes away, too.

Meanwhile, airlines over the past decade have added a premium economy section, which sits between business class and economy. It features recliner seats similar to those in domestic first class, often with foot rests, meals served on actual plates, larger seat-back screens than economy and earlier boarding.

Airlines are now cutting up business class into different segments, something they've done for more than a decade with the coach cabin's basic economy, standard and extra legroom seats.

United and Delta this year each announced their most expensive cabins will be sold with basic options, which are more restrictive and don't include things like the ability to pick your seat ahead of time or get access to a special airport lounge.

According to recent reports, there are also a few seats in some of the business-class cabins that are roomier, like American's Flagship Suite Preferred and United's Polaris Studio. Even the guest seating in the United suite varies with "standard and companion ottomans," the latter including a seatbelt so you can ask "another Polaris passenger to visit you between takeoff and landing for a drink, chat or game," the airline says.

"I don't think we found the limit on segmentation," United CFO Mike Leskinen told CNBC on Thursday. "We have a few things on the drawing board. We're not done.".

Although U.S. carriers are moving away from the designation, first class is far from dead.

Singapore Airlines, Germany's Lufthansa, British Airways and Air France have unveiled updated first-class cabins and other service improvements like food.

British Airways last month said it will build a record 106-suite business class on its Airbus A380 aircraft, the world's largest passenger airplane, but it's also upgrading its first class on board.

Meanwhile, smaller airlines like JetBlue Airways, Frontier Airlines and Allegiant Air are introducing domestic or short-haul first-class seats.

"We're going to be able to do that at a really low price comparatively to what you're used to out there in the marketplace," Frontier Chief Commercial Officer Bobby Schroeter mentioned last month.
